mainTopic: Blemishes on a בכור: on purpose versus by accident, and who is believed about them
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier ruling. If someone made another person's טהרות impure and then died, his son does not pay, because hidden damage is only a rabbinic קנס aimed at the wrongdoer himself. Next comes a new משנה with two stories, a Roman official and children at play. In each one, a בכור got a blemish and the Sages permitted it the first time, but they forbade it when the act was repeated on purpose. The rule is that a blemish made on purpose is forbidden and an accidental one is permitted. The גמרא explains why both stories are needed and debates whether the bystanders' wording can count as encouraging the official. It also explains what the general rule adds: an indirect cause (גרמא) is forbidden, and a blemish that followed offhand talk is permitted. Another משנה permits a בכור that was kicked while chasing its owner, and רב פפא gives two versions about a kick after the chase. The גמרא then discusses making a blemish before the animal is born and a mouth blemish seen only when the animal cries out. Finally, a משנה rules on which shepherds are believed that a blemish was not made on purpose, and רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר begin explaining it in two different ways.

steps.title: The son does not pay for his father's hidden damage
steps.stepSummary: The end of an earlier ruling: if a man made someone else's טהרות impure and then died, his son is not penalized.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person made pure items impure and then died, the Sages did not penalize his son after him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling that started on the previous page: a son does not have to pay for the טהרות his father made impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father himself would have had to pay. Once he dies, though, that duty to pay does not pass to his son. The next steps explain why.

keyTerms.meaning: items kept in a state of ritual purity

phrases.english: If he made pure items impure and died —
they did not penalize his son after him.

steps.triggerLanguage: טִימֵּא טְהָרוֹת וָמֵת — לֹא קָנְסוּ בְּנוֹ אַחֲרָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the sugya from the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An heir is not penalized for the טהרות his father made impure.

steps.title: Asking for the reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the son is not penalized.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ruling. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an heir does pay his father's debts, so it seems strange that this one is different. The question asks what makes this case special.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the ruling in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the son does not have to pay for his father's damage.

steps.title: Hidden damage is only a rabbinic penalty aimed at the person himself
steps.stepSummary: Damage you cannot see is not damage by Torah law. The payment is only a rabbinic קנס, and that קנס was placed on the person who did it, not on his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: Damage that is not visible is not counted as damage. Paying for it is a penalty of the Rabbis, and the Rabbis penalized the person himself, not his son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: making טהרות impure causes no visible change, so the Torah does not count it as damage. The Rabbis made the person pay as a קנס, but only he has to pay, not his son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here is the key point. The payment is not a real Torah debt, so it does not pass down like a regular debt. It is a קנס meant to punish the wrongdoer himself, and his son did nothing wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: damage that cannot be seen, like making something impure
a penalty set up by the Rabbis

steps.whatToRemember: Hidden damage, like making טהרות impure, is not Torah-level damage. The rabbinic קנס falls only on the one who did it, not on his heirs.

phrases.english: Damage that is not visible
is not called damage;
it is a penalty of the Rabbis —
the Rabbis penalized him himself,
his son the Rabbis did not penalize.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר לָא שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because hidden damage is only a rabbinic קנס, and the Rabbis placed it on the person himself, not on his heir.

steps.title: The Roman official who slit a בכור's ear
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells of a Roman official who cut the ear of an old בכור. The first time, the Sages permitted it to be slaughtered. When he cut other בכורות after that, they forbade them.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an old ram with dangling hair. A Roman official saw it and asked what was special about it. They told him it was a בכור, which may only be slaughtered if it has a blemish. He took a dagger and slit its ear. The Sages permitted it. After that, he slit the ears of other בכורות, and the Sages forbade them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a story. A non-Jew made a blemish on a בכור, the Sages permitted it the first time, and they forbade it once he started doing it again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור with a blemish may normally be slaughtered and eaten. The first time, the official did not mean to make the animal permitted: רש״י explains that he did not know a blemish he made would allow it to be slaughtered. Once he began cutting other animals deliberately to make them permitted, the Sages forbade them so people would not make blemishes this way to get an animal permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: a firstborn male animal, which is holy
a blemish; it lets a בכור be slaughtered

steps.confusionAlert: Making a blemish on a בכור is not allowed. That is why the Sages forbade the later animals, even though they really did have a blemish.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
There was an incident with an old male sheep (a ram),
and its hair was dangling,
and a certain Roman official saw it and said:
What is the story of this one?
They said to him: It is a firstborn,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ נִשְׁחָט אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הָיָה בּוֹ מוּם.
phrases.english: and it may not be slaughtered unless it has a blemish.
He took a dagger and slit its ear,
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is the printed spelling, and the word in square brackets is the corrected one. Both mean a dagger.

phrases.english: and the case came before the Sages, and they permitted it,
and after they permitted it,
he went and slit the ears of other firstborns,
and they forbade them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה. The earlier sugya has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blemish made by a non-Jew who did not mean to permit the animal is permitted, but once he makes blemishes on purpose to get permission, those animals are forbidden.

steps.title: The children who tied lambs' tails together
steps.stepSummary: Children at play tied lambs' tails together, and a בכור's tail came off. The Sages permitted it. When people then tied other בכורות's tails on purpose, the Sages forbade them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once, children were playing in a field and tied lambs' tails to each other. One lamb's tail came off, and it was a בכור. The Sages permitted it. People saw that it was permitted, so they went and tied the tails of other בכורות, and the Sages forbade them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second story with the same pattern: the blemish that happened by accident is permitted, and the ones people copied on purpose are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The children did not mean to make a blemish. They were just playing. The ones who copied them, after seeing it permitted, did it in order to make the animals permitted, so the Sages forbade those animals.

phrases.aramaic: פַּעַם אַחַת הָיוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת מְשַׂחֲקִין בַּשָּׂדֶה,
phrases.english: Once, children were playing in the field,
and they tied the tails of lambs to each other,
and the tail of one of them came off,
and it was a firstborn,
and the case came before the Sages, and they permitted it.
They saw that it was permitted,
so they went and tied the tails of other firstborns,
and they forbade them.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת הָיוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת מְשַׂחֲקִין בַּשָּׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story that follows the same pattern as step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blemish that happened by accident during play is permitted, but copying it on purpose is forbidden.

steps.title: The rule: on purpose is forbidden, by accident is permitted
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sums up both stories in one general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: any blemish made on purpose is forbidden, and any blemish made not on purpose is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה turns the two stories into one clear rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What decides the case is intention, not who made the blemish. A blemish made on purpose makes the animal forbidden, and an accidental one leaves the animal permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: A blemish put on a בכור on purpose makes it forbidden. A blemish that happened by accident is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical הלכה for any בכור that got a blemish.

phrases.english: This is the rule:
anything done on purpose is forbidden,
not on purpose is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the two stories in steps 4 and 5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Intention decides: a blemish made on purpose is forbidden, an accidental one is permitted.

steps.title: Why the משנה needs the children's story too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the משנה tells both stories. From the non-Jew alone, one might think the first time is permitted only because he will not form a bad habit. A Jewish child might form that habit, so we would have said not to permit even the first time.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'another time there were children'. Both stories are needed. If the משנה had told us only about the non-Jew, we would say it was permitted because he will not get used to doing it. But a Jewish child might get used to it, so we would say it is not permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an unspoken question: why does the משנה need two stories that seem the same? It begins by showing what the children's story teaches us.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that a Jewish child who sees the first blemish permitted might learn to make blemishes himself. Without the children's story, we might think a child's accidental blemish is forbidden. The second story teaches that it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: it is necessary; both cases are needed
to get used to doing it, to form a habit

steps.confusionAlert: The non-Jew story is told first, but by itself it would not teach the child case. The point is that the habit worry applies only to a Jewish child.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
'Another time there were' and so on.
phrases.notes: This quotes the start of the children's story in the משנה.

phrases.english: And it is necessary,
for if it had taught us only the non-Jew,
that is because he will not come to get used to it,
but a minor, who might come to get used to it,
I would say it is not permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the משנה needs both stories from steps 4 and 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each case teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only the non-Jew story, we might think a child's accidental blemish is forbidden, because the child might form a habit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The children's story teaches that even a child's first accidental blemish is permitted.

steps.title: Why the children's story alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the צריכותא. Had the משנה told only the children's story, we might think it is permitted there because no one confuses a child with an adult. A non-Jewish adult could be confused with a Jewish adult, so we might forbid even the first time. That is why both stories are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had told us only about the child, we might say it is permitted because people will not mix up a child with an adult. But with a non-Jew, people might mix him up with a Jewish adult, so I would say it is not permitted. So both stories are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer it started in step 7. It shows why the children's story could not teach us the official's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 showed that the official's story could not teach us the children's case. Now we see the reverse. A child's act will not lead people to think adults may make blemishes. A non-Jewish adult's act might, because people could confuse him with a Jewish adult. Each story has its own reason to forbid, so each one is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A minor, a child under the age of מצוות
To be confused with or mixed up with
It is necessary, so both cases must be taught

steps.whatToRemember: Each story has a different possible reason to forbid even the first time: the child might form a habit, and the non-Jew might be confused with a Jewish adult. So the משנה needs both stories to show that the first time is permitted in each case.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only the minor,
phrases.notes: This means the story of the children who tied the lambs' tails together.

phrases.english: we might say it is permitted because people will not come to confuse him with an adult,
but a non-Jew, whom people may come to confuse with a [Jewish] adult —
I would say it is not permitted.
So it is necessary to teach both.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second half of the צריכותא begun in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case teaches something the other could not
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the children's story alone, we might permit only there and forbid the non-Jew even the first time, because people could confuse him with a Jewish adult.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both stories are needed. In each case the first, unplanned time is permitted.

steps.title: The bystanders' wording can make the blemish count as encouraged
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting רב קטינא, limits the official's case. It was permitted only because the people told him 'not unless it had a מום.' If they had said 'only if a מום is made in it,' that is like telling him to go make a מום, and the animal would be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב קטינא: They only taught this where people told the official, 'Not unless it had a blemish.' But if they told him, 'If a blemish is made in it,' that is as if they told him, 'Go make a blemish in it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא brings רב קטינא's ruling. It limits when the official's first cut is permitted, based on the exact words the Jews said to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'It had a מום' sounds like a blemish that comes by itself. 'A מום is made in it' sounds like a blemish that someone makes. Saying the second version invites the official to cut the animal, so the cut counts as done for the Jews' sake, and the animal is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of, a phrase that limits a ruling
It had a blemish, which sounds like it came by itself
A blemish was made in it, which could sound like someone made it
Go make a blemish in it, a direct instruction

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said that Rav Ketina said:
They taught this only
phrases.notes: This goes back to the story of the Roman official in step 4.

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ ״אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הָיָה בּוֹ מוּם״,
phrases.english: where they told him, 'Not unless it had a blemish,'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִם אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ ״אִם נַעֲשָׂה בּוֹ מוּם״ —
phrases.english: but if they told him, 'If a blemish is made in it' —

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן דַּאֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ ״זִיל עֲבֵיד בֵּיהּ מוּמָא״ דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: it is as if they told him, 'Go make a blemish in it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the צריכותא and returns to the official's story to limit when it applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first cut is permitted only if the Jews said 'unless it had a מום.' Saying 'if a מום is made in it' counts as encouraging him, and the animal is forbidden.

steps.title: רבא: both wordings mean the blemish came by itself
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with רב קטינא. Both 'it had' and 'it was made' describe a blemish that happens by itself. So there is no difference between them, and in both cases the animal is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: After all, it means it happened by itself. What difference is it to me whether they said 'had' or 'was made'? Rather, 'was made' also means by itself, and there is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects רב קטינא's split between the two wordings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב קטינא heard 'a מום was made' as a hint to go make one. רבא says that phrase is passive and does not ask anyone to act. So it means the same as 'it had a מום,' and both are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: After all, consider this, a phrase that opens a logical point
By itself, with no one causing it on purpose
What difference is it to me

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying that telling someone 'go make a מום' is permitted. He agrees that would be forbidden. He only argues that the words 'a מום was made' are not such an instruction.

phrases.english: Rava said: After all, it means by itself,
what difference is it to me whether 'had' or 'was made'?
Rather, 'was made' also means by itself,
and there is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב קטינא's split between the wordings in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב קטינא's distinction between 'היה בו מום' and 'נעשה בו מום'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'נעשה' is passive and describes a blemish that happens by itself. It is not an instruction to cause one.

steps.title: What does the general rule come to add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule, 'anything done on purpose is forbidden,' and asks what extra case this rule includes.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the general rule: anything done on purpose is forbidden. What does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the משנה's general rule from step 6. It asks what the rule adds beyond the two stories, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'זה הכלל' usually signals that the משנה wants to include a case not stated openly. So the גמרא looks for what new case the rule covers.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it come to include?

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁהוּא לְדַעַת — אָסוּר.
phrases.english: This is the general rule: anything that is done on purpose is forbidden.
What does it come to include?

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁהוּא לְדַעַת — אָסוּר. לְאֵיתוֹיֵי מַאי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the wording debate and returns to the משנה's general rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case the rule 'כל שהוא לדעת אסור' is meant to include.

steps.title: The rule includes a blemish caused indirectly
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the rule includes גרמא, a blemish caused indirectly. Even if the person did not make the blemish with his own hands, if he caused it on purpose, the animal is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include an indirect cause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the general rule includes a blemish that a person causes indirectly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think only a direct cut counts as 'on purpose.' The rule teaches that causing a blemish indirectly, but on purpose, is treated the same way, so the animal still may not be slaughtered because of it.

keyTerms.meaning: An indirect cause, bringing about a result without doing it directly

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's rule 'anything done on purpose is forbidden' covers even a blemish caused indirectly (גרמא), not only one made directly.
steps.whyThisMatters: This makes the ban wider. A person cannot get around it by causing a blemish indirectly instead of making it himself.

phrases.english: It comes to include an indirect cause.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The general rule includes גרמא. A blemish caused indirectly on purpose also makes the animal forbidden.

steps.title: What 'without intent' comes to include
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the משנה's rule, 'without intent, it is permitted,' includes a case where a non-Jew learned about the בכור from someone speaking offhandedly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The words 'without intent' come to include someone who speaks innocently, without any plan.
steps.whatsHappening: Just as it did for 'on purpose,' the גמרא asks what 'without intent' adds, and answers in one short line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the non-Jew made the מום on purpose, but the Jew never pushed him to do it. He only overheard the Jews themselves chatting offhandedly about the בכור. Since they did not mean for him to make a מום, the animal is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: One who speaks innocently, just chatting, with no hidden aim

steps.whatToRemember: 'On purpose' includes even an indirect cause (גרמא). 'Without intent' includes a case where the information came out in offhand talk. What counts is whether the owner meant for a מום to happen.

phrases.english: [The words] 'without intent':
come to include one who speaks offhandedly.
phrases.notes: The non-Jew did not ask. The Jews themselves were just chatting, with no plan for him to make a מום (רש״י).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels steps 11 and 12. After explaining 'on purpose,' the גמרא now explains 'without intent.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A case where the non-Jew learned about the בכור from someone speaking offhandedly, so the animal is permitted.

steps.title: The משנה: a בכור that chased its owner and was kicked
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that if a בכור chased its owner, and he kicked it and caused a מום, he may slaughter it because of that מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a firstborn animal was chasing a person, and he kicked it and gave it a blemish, he may slaughter it because of that blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives a case where the owner himself caused the מום, and still the animal is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a מום made on purpose makes the בכור forbidden. Here the kick was self-defense against an animal chasing him, not a plan to make a מום, so the משנה permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn animal, which is holy and may only be slaughtered outside the מקדש if it has a מום

phrases.english: MISHNA: If a firstborn animal was chasing him,
and he kicked it and made a blemish in it,
he may slaughter it on account of that blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה that fits the same theme of a מום that was not made on purpose.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מום caused by kicking a בכור that was chasing you is permitted, and the animal may be slaughtered.

steps.title: רב פפא: only a kick during the chase
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא limits the משנה. It is permitted only if he kicked the animal while it was chasing him, not after the chase was over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The משנה only allowed it when he kicked it during the chase. But if he kicked it after the chase, it is not allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא narrows the משנה's ruling to a kick that happened while the chase was still going on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During the chase, the kick is plain self-defense. Once the chase is over, there is no need to defend himself, so a kick then looks like he meant to make a מום. That makes it forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when... (a phrase that limits a ruling)

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּעָטוֹ בִּשְׁעַת רְדִיפָה,
phrases.english: They taught this only where he kicked it during the chase,
but after the chase, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the משנה from step 14 to a kick during the chase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a kick during the chase is permitted. A kick after the chase makes the בכור forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't רב פפא's point obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: of course a kick after the chase is forbidden, so why say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to teach this at all. It seems clear without him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the chase there is no danger, so kicking the animal looks like making a מום on purpose. That falls right into the rule that a מום done on purpose is forbidden. So רב פפא seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's limit from step 15 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's statement that a kick after the chase is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A kick after the chase is clearly on purpose, and a מום made on purpose is already known to be forbidden. So the statement seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Why רב פפא's point is needed: the anger idea
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought a kick after the chase was just anger at the pain the animal caused, not a plan to make a מום. רב פפא teaches that it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: he was remembering his pain, and kicked out of anger. So רב פפא teaches us that it is still forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' challenge by showing a mistaken idea that רב פפא comes to block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could argue the owner kicked after the chase only because he was still upset, not to make a מום. Then it would not count as on purpose. רב פפא rules that we do not accept this excuse, and the animal is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken thought)

steps.whatToRemember: In this first version of רב פפא, a kick during the chase is self-defense, so it is permitted. A kick after the chase is treated as making a מום on purpose, even though he could say he was just angry, so it is forbidden. The next step brings a second version that rules the other way.

phrases.english: You might have said:
it is his pain that he remembers,
so he teaches us [that it is forbidden].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'it's obvious' challenge from step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: showing a reasonable mistaken idea that the statement comes to block
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A kick after the chase might be only anger at the pain he remembers, so the animal would be permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: We do not accept the anger excuse. A kick after the chase counts as making a מום on purpose, and the בכור is forbidden.

steps.title: Second version: kicking even after the chase is allowed
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רב פפא says it is permitted even if he kicked the בכור after the chase, because he was reacting to the pain he remembered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב פפא said, don't think that only a kick during the chase is allowed and a kick not during the chase is not. Even after the chase it is allowed too. Why? He remembers his pain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of רב פפא's teaching from Step 15, and here he rules the opposite way: even a kick after the chase is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, a kick after the chase looked like a plan to make a מום, so it was forbidden. In this version, we say the owner was still upset about the pain the animal caused him, so the kick is not a plan to make a מום. That makes it fit the משנה's case of a kick without intent.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions use the same reason, the owner's anger at his pain. In the first version (Step 17) that reason was rejected and the kick was forbidden. In this version the same reason is accepted and the kick is permitted.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Rav Pappa said:
Do not say: at the time of the chase, yes,
but not at the time of the chase, no;
rather, even after the chase it is allowed too.
What is the reason?
It is his pain that he remembers.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording. Either way it means the kick came from his hurt feelings, not a plan to make a מום.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא תֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version of רב פפא's limit from Steps 15-17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a kick after the chase is permitted, since the owner is assumed to be reacting to his pain and not planning a מום.

steps.title: A blemish may be made before the בכור is born
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that one may make a מום in a בכור before it comes out into the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: It is permitted to make a blemish in a בכור before it comes out into the air of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. רב יהודה allows making a מום in a בכור while it is still being born, before it has fully come out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally it is forbidden to put a מום on a בכור. רב יהודה teaches that this ban only starts once the animal has come out into the world. Before that point, making a מום is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Before it came out into the air of the world, meaning before it is fully born

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling sets up the practical question in the next steps: which part of the animal can be reached while it is still being born?

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
It is permitted to make a blemish in a firstborn animal
before it comes out into the air of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: מוּתָּר לְהַטִּיל מוּם בִּבְכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching on the same broad topic of making a מום in a בכור.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Making a מום in a בכור is permitted before it emerges into the world.

steps.title: Where to make the blemish: a kid's ear, a lamb's lip
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that a young goat can be blemished on its ear, and a lamb on its lip.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A kid, on its ear. A lamb, on its lips.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא applies רב יהודה's rule and tells us which body part to blemish while the animal is being born.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only a part of the body that shows before the birth is finished can be blemished in time. For a kid, רבא says this is the ear. For a lamb, he says it is the lip.

phrases.english: Rava said:
A kid: on its ear;
phrases.notes: He means this is the place where you can make the מום while it is being born.

phrases.english: a lamb: on its lips.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts רב יהודה's rule into practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A kid may be blemished on its ear, and a lamb on its lip, before birth is complete.

steps.title: Second version: a lamb's ear works too
steps.stepSummary: A second version says a lamb can also be blemished on its ear, since it may come out with the sides of its head first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: A lamb also on its ear, since we can say it came out by way of its temples.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of רבא's words, in which a lamb is treated like a kid and can be blemished on its ear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version limited a lamb to its lip. This version says a lamb may come out with the sides of its head first, so its ear can also be reached before birth is complete.

keyTerms.meaning: Its temples (the sides of the head)

phrases.english: There are those who say:
A lamb too: on its ear,
since we can say it came out by way of its temples.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternate version of רבא's ruling in Step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lamb may also be blemished on its ear, since it may emerge with the sides of its head first.

steps.title: A blemish seen only when the animal cries out counts
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a mouth blemish that is hidden while the animal eats, but shows when it opens wide to cry out, is a real מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If it is not seen when the animal eats, but it is seen when it cries out, it is a blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רבא about a blemish inside the mouth that only shows some of the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether a blemish must be visible all the time to count. רבא says it is enough that it shows when the animal opens its mouth wide to cry out. That makes the בכור fit to be slaughtered.

keyTerms.meaning: Cries out (bleats), opening its mouth wide

phrases.english: Rava said:
If when it eats it is not seen,
but when it cries out it is seen,
it is a blemish.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אָכֵל וְלָא מִיחֲזֵי, פָּעֵי וּמִיחֲזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic: what counts as a visible מום.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blemish seen only when the animal opens its mouth to cry out still counts as a מום.

steps.title: Why say it? A משנה already teaches this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבא adds, since a משנה already counts pulled-out inner gums as a מום, and those can only be seen when the animal cries out.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבא teaching us? We already learned in a משנה: the outer gums that were damaged or scraped, and the inner gums that were pulled out. What is the reason the inner ones count? Isn't it because they are seen when the animal cries out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא and says his ruling is not new, because a משנה already teaches it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists inner gums that were pulled out as a מום. Inner gums cannot be seen while the animal eats, only when it opens wide to cry out. So the משנה already seems to say exactly what רבא said.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (asked when a teaching seems to add nothing new)

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה later in the tractate that lists the blemishes of a בכור.

phrases.english: the outer gums that were damaged or that were scraped,
and the inner ones that were pulled out.
What is the reason?
Is it not because it is seen when it cries out?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling from Step 22 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that a blemish seen only when the animal cries out is a מום
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already treats pulled-out inner gums as a מום, and those are only seen when the animal cries out, so רבא's ruling adds nothing.

steps.title: רבא is explaining the reason of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that רבא was not adding a new law. He was explaining why pulled-out inner gums count as a מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: רבא is also explaining the reason of the משנה. Why do pulled-out gums count as a blemish? Because they are seen when the animal cries out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge: רבא's words are an explanation of the משנה's reason, not a separate new ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed רבא meant to teach something new. רב פפא agrees that the law is already in the משנה. He says רבא was spelling out its reason: a blemish counts as long as it can be seen when the animal opens its mouth wide.
steps.whatToRemember: A mouth blemish counts as a מום even if it shows only when the animal opens wide to cry out. רבא did not add a new law; he explained the reason behind the משנה about pulled-out inner gums.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Rava too is explaining the reason of the Mishnah:
what is the reason that pulled-out gums are a blemish?
Because when it cries out, it is seen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: רָבָא נָמֵי טַעְמָא דְמַתְנִיתִין מְפָרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the statement as an explanation of the משנה's reason rather than a new law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא was teaching a new law that the משנה already covered, which would make his statement unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא was explaining the משנה's reason: a blemish counts if it is seen when the animal cries out.

steps.title: The new משנה: Israelite shepherds are believed, priest shepherds are not
steps.stepSummary: For blemishes a person could cause, Israelite shepherds are believed to say the blemish happened by itself. Priest shepherds are not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: For any blemish that a person could have caused, Israelite shepherds are believed, but priest shepherds are not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on whose word we accept when a בכור has a blemish that someone could have made on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור with a blemish may be eaten by a כהן, but only if nobody made the blemish on purpose. An Israelite shepherd gains nothing from the blemish, so we trust him. A כהן could end up eating the animal, so he has a reason to lie, and we do not trust him.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה, the base text the גמרא will discuss
A blemish on an animal that disqualifies it as a קרבן
By a person's hands, meaning on purpose and not by nature

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the whole sugya. Trust depends on whether the witness gains anything from the blemish.

phrases.english: MISHNA: All the blemishes
that are able to come about by a person's hands,
Israelite shepherds are believed,
priest shepherds are not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ כׇּל הַמּוּמִין הָרְאוּיִין לָבֹא בִּידֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the discussion of mouth blemishes ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For man-made-type blemishes, Israelite shepherds are believed; priest shepherds are not.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: a כהן is believed about someone else's animal
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says a כהן is believed about another person's בכור but not about his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He is believed about his friend's animal, but not about his own.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה makes the rule about כהנים narrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion did not trust any כהן. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל distrusts a כהן only when the animal is his own, because only then does he clearly gain.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
he is believed about that of his friend,
phrases.notes: "He" is the כהן, and "that of his friend" means someone else's בכור.

phrases.english: but is not believed about his own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion by trusting a כהן about someone else's animal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is believed about another's בכור, not about his own.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: someone suspected in a matter cannot judge or testify about it
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says a person suspected about a matter may neither judge nor testify about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: Someone suspected about a matter may not judge it and may not testify about it.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion in the משנה gives a broad rule against trusting a suspected person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר goes further than רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. A כהן who is suspected of making blemishes cannot rule on or testify about this kind of case at all, even for someone else's animal.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three views in the משנה. First, no priest shepherd is believed. Second, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says a כהן is believed only for others. Third, רבי מאיר says a suspected person cannot judge or testify in this matter at all.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
one who is suspected about the matter
may neither judge it nor testify about it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר הֶחָשׁוּד עַל הַדֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a stricter general rule than רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A suspected person may neither judge nor testify about that matter.

steps.title: First reading: Israelite shepherds working for a כהן are still believed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree about the משנה. One says the Israelite shepherds work for a כהן and are still believed, because a small reward will not make them lie.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree. One says: "Israelite shepherds" means those working for כהנים, and they are believed. We do not worry that they would lie for a small taste of the meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the משנה. It brings a disagreement and starts with the first view of what case the משנה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An Israelite working for a כהן might seem to have a motive, since the כהן could reward him with a bite of the בכור. This view says such a tiny gain is not enough to make him lie, so he is believed. The other view in this disagreement begins in step 33.

keyTerms.meaning: The household of כהנים, meaning working for a כהן
A swallow, a small taste of food

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree.
One says:
"Israelite shepherds" means those in the household of כהנים,
and they are believed,
since we are not worried about a swallow.
phrases.notes: The worry would be that the כהן rewards them with a taste of the meat. That small gain is not enough to make them lie.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא's explanation of the first ruling in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Israelite shepherds working for a כהן are believed, because a small taste is not a real motive.

steps.title: Priest shepherds working for an Israelite are not believed
steps.stepSummary: In the same view, a כהן working for an Israelite is not believed. He expects the owner to give the בכור to him because he took care of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Priest shepherds working for an Israelite are not believed. A כהן like that thinks: since I worked hard on this animal, the owner will not skip me and give it to another כהן.
steps.whatsHappening: The same view now explains the second half of the משנה, about priest shepherds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Israelite owner can choose which כהן gets his בכור. A כהן who cared for the animal expects to be chosen, so he gains a whole animal from a blemish. That is a real motive, so we do not trust him.

keyTerms.meaning: The household of an Israelite, meaning working for him
He will not leave aside, skip over

phrases.english: Priest shepherds in the household of an Israelite
are not believed,
because he says to himself:
"Since I put effort into it,
he will not leave me aside
phrases.notes: "He" is the Israelite owner, who picks which כהן receives his בכור.

phrases.english: and give it to others."

steps.triggerLanguage: רוֹעֵי כֹּהֲנִים בֵּי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין נֶאֱמָנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same view, now explaining priest shepherds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A priest shepherd working for an Israelite is not believed, because he expects to receive the בכור.

steps.title: One כהן is not believed for another כהן, because they may trade favors
steps.stepSummary: The same view adds that a כהן is not believed about another כהן's animal, because the two might lie for each other in turn.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same law applies to a כהן testifying for another כהן. He is not believed, because we worry they will repay each other's favors.
steps.whatsHappening: The same view adds one more case. Even a כהן who gains nothing right now is not trusted about another כהן's בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry here is not a direct reward. One כהן might lie today so the other כהן will lie for him later. Notice that this does not trust a כהן about someone else's animal, even though רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in the משנה did.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a future return favor can also count as a motive that makes a witness untrustworthy.

phrases.english: And the same is true of a כהן for a כהן,
since we are concerned about repaying favors.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהוּא הַדִּין כֹּהֵן לְכֹהֵן דְּחָיְישִׁינַן לְגוֹמְלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the same view's distrust of כהנים to a כהן testifying for another כהן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is not believed for another כהן, because of the worry about returned favors.

steps.title: In the first reading, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל believes a כהן about another כהן's animal
steps.stepSummary: Inside the first אמורא's explanation, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל comes to argue: a כהן is believed about his friend's בכור, just not about his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל comes to say: he is believed about his friend's animal, but not about his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still explaining the משנה according to the first אמורא. It now shows what רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds to that reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 30, the first reading said a כהן is not believed about another כהן's animal, because they might cover for each other. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees and does not worry about that. He only refuses to believe a כהן about his own בכור, where the gain to himself is direct.

keyTerms.meaning: And he comes to say. It shows what this opinion adds or disputes.
His friend's, meaning another person's animal

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new statement by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. It is the same words from step 26, now read through the first אמורא's explanation, so they become a disagreement with the תנא קמא about another כהן's animal.

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲתָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לְמֵימַר:
phrases.english: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comes to say:
he is believed about that of his friend,
but he is not believed about his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲתָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the תנא קמא as explained in step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is believed about another כהן's בכור, but not about his own.

steps.title: In the first reading, רבי מאיר says a suspected person may not judge or testify at all
steps.stepSummary: Inside the same reading, רבי מאיר comes to say: someone suspected about a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר comes to say: one who is suspected about the matter may not judge it and may not testify about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the first אמורא's reading by showing where רבי מאיר stands. He is the strictest voice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל believed a כהן about another כהן's animal. רבי מאיר says that a כהן is suspected of making blemishes, so he cannot judge or testify about blemishes for anyone, even a stranger. (The גמרא will explain later how he differs from the תנא קמא.)

keyTerms.meaning: Someone suspected about a particular matter
Judges it, rules on it as a judge
Testifies about it as a witness

steps.whatToRemember: First reading: the תנא קמא does not believe a כהן about another כהן's animal. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does believe him about another's animal, just not his own. רבי מאיר says a suspected person may never judge or testify on that matter.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir comes to say:
one who is suspected about the matter
may neither judge it nor testify about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the first reading by placing רבי מאיר's stricter view next to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person suspected about a matter may not serve as judge or witness on it, even for someone else.

steps.title: The second reading: the 'Israelite shepherds' are כהנים, and they are believed
steps.stepSummary: The other אמורא reads 'Israelite shepherds' as כהנים who work as shepherds for an Israelite. The משנה says they are believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one says: 'Israelite shepherds' means the shepherds are כהנים working for Israelites, and they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now opens the second אמורא's explanation of the משנה. It starts by redefining who the 'Israelite shepherds' are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first reading, the shepherds were Israelites working for a כהן. Here it is flipped: the shepherds are כהנים and the owner is an Israelite. Even so, the משנה believes them that the blemish was not made on purpose. They are not suspected of lying just to get the meat.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one says. It brings the second of the two views.
Israelite shepherds, the phrase from the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two readings. In the first, the shepherds are Israelites. In the second, the shepherds are כהנים and the owner is an Israelite, and they are still believed.

phrases.english: And the other one says: "Israelite shepherds"
phrases.notes: This is the other of the two אמוראים from step 28, רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר.

phrases.english: and they are priests: they are believed,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחַד אָמַר רוֹעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהֵן כֹּהֲנִים נֶאֱמָנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first reading is complete, this begins the competing explanation of the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כהנים who work as shepherds for an Israelite's בכור are believed that its blemish was not made on purpose.
